input: According to NASA SAFFIRE research (NASA/TM-20205008182), what happens to the flame when ventilation velocity is near zero in microgravity?
context: [NASA/TM-20205008182 | DOI:10.60555/0t15-1z43] Saffire-I on Cygnus demonstrated that large-scale Cotton-Fiberglass SIBAL fabric (0.4 m wide by 1.0 m long) burned continuously under microgravity with a forced flow of 0.2 m/s. Flame spread rate reached ~2.1 mm/s in concurrent flow. Radiation from the large flame zone to the unburned fuel preheats the fuel bed more significantly than in bench-scale ISS glovebox tests.
target: Based on NASA SAFFIRE findings (NASA/TM-20205008182), under quiescent microgravity conditions (forced flow < 0.02 m/s), flames cannot sustain steady combustion and tend to self-extinguish. This occurs because without natural buoyancy, combustion products accumulate spherically around the reaction zone, causing localized oxygen starvation.

input: Explain to a high-school physics student why gravity changes the shape of a flame based on NASA SAFFIRE studies.
context: [NASA/TM-20205008182] Saffire-I on Cygnus demonstrated that large-scale Cotton-Fiberglass SIBAL fabric (0.4 m wide by 1.0 m long) burned continuously under microgravity with a forced flow of 0.2 m/s. Flame spread rate reached ~2.1 mm/s in concurrent flow. Radiation from the large flame zone to the unburned fuel preheats the fuel bed more significantly than in bench-scale ISS glovebox tests.
target: On Earth, hot air is lighter than cold air, so buoyancy pulls hot gases upward into a familiar teardrop flame. In space (microgravity), there is no buoyancy. As NASA SAFFIRE (NASA/TM-20205008182) observed, heat only moves outward via slow molecular diffusion, creating a rounded, spherical flame. Without airflow, it suffocates in its own exhaust gases.

context: [NASA/TM-20205008182 | DOI:10.60555/0t15-1z43] Saffire-II tested exploration atmospheres: under 34% elevated oxygen and 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia) reduced pressure matching Artemis Lunar exploration baselines, solid materials ignition delay shortened by 40%, and flame spread rate increased by 2.4-fold compared to standard Earth-sea-level air. Low pressure reduces total heat capacity of gas, while elevated oxygen fraction broadens flammability limits.

input: According to NASA BASS_II research (NASA/TM-2016-219083), what happens to the flame when ventilation velocity is near zero in microgravity?
context: [NASA/TM-2016-219083 | DOI:10.60555/4qc4-de67] In the Microgravity Science Glovebox on ISS, BASS-II investigated thick PMMA slabs and thin films. In quiescent microgravity (forced flow < 0.02 m/s), flames consistently self-extinguished even in 25% oxygen due to spherical accumulation of combustion products (CO2 and H2O) causing oxygen starvation. A critical low-speed extinction boundary exists below which steady combustion cannot be sustained.

context: [NASA/TM-2016-219083 | DOI:10.60555/4qc4-de67] BASS-II PMMA combustion tests generated significant carbon monoxide (CO) concentrations reaching up to 360 ppm in localized chamber volumes when burning thick fuel. Delrin (polyoxymethylene) tests yielded formaldehyde decomposition hazards. For human spacecraft fire safety, toxic gas accumulation during smoldering or low-flow burning presents an immediate crew life-support risk before large thermal release occurs.
